definition.text: A tax on the rent, or surplus profit, earned by exploiting a natural resource, which can apply to renewable and non-renewable resources.

facts.text: It taxes the surplus beyond the necessary costs of production, including a reward to capital.
Investors pay nothing until they reach a set rate of return; after that, profits are shared with the host government.
It is most common in mining and petroleum; Norway has also applied it to fish farming from 2023 and onshore wind from 2024, Iceland to fishing and Switzerland to hydropower.

definition.text: A tax charged on removing natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, uranium or timber within a taxing jurisdiction.

facts.text: It is used where resources are privately owned, as in the United States; where resources are publicly owned, a resource royalty is paid instead, called stumpage in forestry.
As of 2021, 34 US states collected a severance tax on oil and gas.
Some states put the revenue into permanent endowments, from about $800 million in Montana to more than $37 billion in Alaska, meant to outlast extraction.
Severance taxes are counted among environmental taxes and cited as classic Pigouvian taxes.

title: Simon–Ehrlich wager

definition.text: A 1980 bet between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich on whether natural resources would become scarcer, measured by metal prices up to 1990.

facts.text: Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb (1968), expected resources to be outstripped by population growth; Simon bet that raw material prices would not rise in the long run.
Ehrlich chose copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, buying $200 of each on paper on 29 September 1980, with payoff on 29 September 1990.
All five fell in inflation-adjusted price even though world population grew by more than 800 million, and Ehrlich paid Simon $576.07.
Over 1980–2011 Simon would have lost on four of the five metals, and one study found he would have won in only 38.4% of periods from 1900 to 2008.
Some analysts conclude the bet shows luck mattered more than expertise, and does not prove there are no environmental limits to growth.
Simon declined Ehrlich and Schneider's later offer to bet on 15 environmental trends; he would have lost on 11 of them.

contested_note: Observers disagree on what the wager proves, since the result depends heavily on the time period chosen.

definition.text: A state-owned investment fund that invests in assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate and precious metals.

facts.text: Most are funded by commodity export revenues or by central bank foreign exchange reserves, and many were set up by oil-rich states.
For commodity-exporting countries, a fund can smooth volatile government revenue and save for the longer term.
The first for a sovereign state was the Kuwait Investment Authority, created from oil revenues in 1953.
Assets under management reached $13–15 trillion by 2025; funds built on oil and gas exports held $5.4 trillion as of 2020.
The 24 Santiago Principles, drafted in 2008 under IMF leadership, set standards for transparency, independence and accountability.
Many funds have been exhausted, mainly because of political instability rather than economic factors.
